newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro court rules Britain wrongly bugged police boss.
newsitem.headline: Euro court rules Britain wrongly bugged police boss.

text.p: The European Court of Human Rights ruled on Wednesday that Britain violated the rights of a female police chief by bugging her phone at work after she filed a suit alleging sex discrimination.

The nine judges ordered Britain to pay Alison Halford, once the highest ranking female police officer in Britain, 10,000 pounds ($16,500) for violating her right to a private life. It also awarded her some costs after a six-year legal marathon.
The unanimous ruling by the Strasbourg-based court, part of the 40-nation Council of Europe, could force Britain to modify its phone-tapping rules.

The court said Britain tapped Halford's phone at work when she was Merseyside assistant chief constable in northern England, after she filed a lawsuit in 1990 alleging her further promotion was blocked by sex discrimination.

The bugging was "probably with the primary aim of gathering material to assist in the defence of the sex discrimination proceedings against them," the Council of Europe said. Halford had unsuccessfully applied for several jobs as chief constable.
Britain argued police could tap their internal telephones without a warrant since there were no limits on such bugging in a 1985 phone-tap law.

"It was clear from the court's case law that telephone calls made from business premises as well as from the home might be covered by the notion of 'private life,'" the Council of Europe said, summing up the judgment.

But the court dismissed Halford's claims that her phone at home had also been bugged. Britain merely admitted at the hearings that there had been a "reasonable likelihood" her work phone was bugged, but not her home phone.
Halford, now 57, withdrew her sex discrimination case in 1992, agreeing to retire under a deal in which she received 15,000 pounds ($25,000).

Apart from 10,000 pounds for intrusion into Halford's private life, the court also awarded Halford 600 pounds ($1,000) towards personal expenses and 25,000 ($41,600) of the 142,875 pounds ($237,900) she claimed in legal costs.
